tool.name: ExtractSlopeValuesToPoints

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/topographic-analysis/extract-slope-values-to-points.html
Adds a field holding the slope at each point, extracted from a slope raster, to a copy of the input point features or to the input feature class itself. Nearly identical to Esri's Extract Values to Points, except that the optional interpolation is computed on the slope angles (so percent slopes are never averaged raw), the field can be added to the existing point features under a name you choose, and no extension license is required. The raster can also be a DEM: the slope is then computed at each point by Horn's 3 x 3 method (the method of Esri's Slope tool) or a least-squares quadratic over a chosen window, over true ground distances in any coordinate system.

tool.usage:
How it differs from Esri's tool. Esri's Extract Values to Points does three things this tool also does: it finds the cell each point falls in, it optionally interpolates from the four surrounding cell centers, and it writes the value to a new field of a copy of the points. The differences are that this tool interpolates slope correctly whatever unit the raster is in, that it can add the field to the input feature class instead of copying it (Esri's tool always makes a copy; its Extract Multi Values to Points writes into the input but offers no interpolation of this kind), that the field is named as you choose rather than RASTERVALU, and that it needs no Spatial Analyst license.
Why interpolate on the angles. Percent slope is 100 times the rise over the run, and rise over run is the tangent of the slope angle. The tangent grows faster and faster as the angle steepens (a convex function), so averaging raw percent values weights the steep cells more than the gentle ones and the result comes out too steep. A point midway between cells of 50 and 70 degrees (119.2% and 274.7%) has a true interpolated slope of 60 degrees, which is 173.2%; averaging the two percent values gives 197.0%, which is a 63.1-degree slope, three degrees too steep. With interpolation on, this tool converts each of the four neighboring cells to its angle first (the arctangent for percent and rise:run, a rescaling for gradians), interpolates the angles with the standard bilinear weights, and converts the result back to the raster's unit. A degree raster and a percent raster of the same ground therefore give the same answer, one in degrees and the other as its tangent times 100. See the Slope Zonal Statistics as Table help for the same rule applied to zonal statistics.
Extraction options. With interpolation off (the default, matching Esri's default) each point receives the value of the raster cell it falls in, exactly as stored, in the raster's own unit; nothing is converted. With interpolation on, each point receives the bilinear interpolation of the four surrounding cell centers computed on the slope angles as described above. NoData neighbors are excluded and the weights renormalized over the remaining neighbors, as are neighbors whose values fall outside the valid range for the chosen unit (beyond plus or minus 90 degrees, or plus or minus 100 gon; percent and rise:run have no limit). Points on NoData or outside the raster receive NULL in a geodatabase output, or -9999 in a shapefile (which cannot store null).
Units and how they are detected. The Slope units of the input raster drop-down offers degrees, percent slope, rise:run ratio and gradians. Esri's Slope and Surface Parameters tools record their output unit (DEGREE or PERCENT_RISE) in the geoprocessing history stored in the raster's metadata, and the tool reads that history when you pick a raster and sets the drop-down to match; when the history says nothing, the drop-down falls back to Degrees. If the history records one unit and you choose another, the dialog warns, the tool runs with the unit you chose, and the same warning is written to the run report and into the new field's metadata. Values outside the valid range for the chosen unit are counted and reported with a warning that the raster may not be a slope raster in that unit.
Where the values go. A new point feature class: a copy of the input points (an active selection and definition query are honored) carrying all the input attributes plus the new DOUBLE field. A new field in the input feature class: the field is added to the input itself and no copy is made; the points the layer shows (its selection and definition query) receive values and any other rows of the feature class are left NULL, and the run report says how many. A layer with a join cannot take a new field. In either case the field is named "Slope" unless you choose another name; a name that is not valid for the workspace, or is already taken, is adjusted (Slope_2, Slope_3, ...) and the run messages report the name actually used. The field's metadata records the unit, the NULL or -9999 convention, the extraction method, the source raster and any unit warning.
Coordinate systems. The points are read in the raster's coordinate system (the raster is never projected; reprojecting point coordinates is exact, and when the datums differ a datum transformation is applied and named in the run messages), and the raster is read only over the points' extent, so large regional rasters are handled efficiently. Projected and geographic rasters both work.
Computing from a DEM. Set What the raster holds to Elevation (DEM) and the tool derives the slope itself, at exactly the cells the sampling step needs, so the numbers are the same as making a slope raster first and extracting from it. The default Horn (3 x 3) method is the third-order finite difference used by Esri's Slope and Aspect tools (planar method), down to their NoData rule; on a projection that is true to scale, such as UTM or State Plane, the values are identical to extracting from an Esri planar slope raster. The difference is that the distances between cells are measured on the spheroid, whatever the coordinate system, so a Web Mercator or a lat/long DEM gives correct slopes too (see the help site's page on projection distortion). The Quadratic least squares method fits the Evans-Young quadratic surface to a window of 3 to 15 cells and takes the slope from its first derivatives at the center: at 3 x 3 it is the equal-weight estimator (slightly less noise-tolerant than Horn), and a wider window smooths and generalizes, which suits fine-resolution lidar DEMs. Comparisons in the literature (Skidmore 1989; Jones 1998; Florinsky 1998; Zhou and Liu 2004; Evans 2013) find Horn's 3 x 3 method a highly accurate estimator in practice: second only to the four-cell method on error-free surfaces and among the least sensitive to DEM error. Elevation units default from the DEM's vertical coordinate system when it has one. Slope units then give the unit of the computed values. To extract values computed exactly as Esri's Surface Parameters tool computes them (its quadratic or biquadratic fit in geocentric coordinates), run Surface Parameters first and extract from its raster.
This tool honors no geoprocessing environments. Esri's Extract Values to Points is documented in the ArcGIS Pro tool reference (Spatial Analyst toolbox).

dialogReference.para: The point features to extract slope values for. An active selection and a definition query are honored. Must be a single-point feature class (multipoint is not supported).

param.name: in_raster
param.displayname: Input slope raster or DEM (single band)

dialogReference.para: A single-band slope raster in degrees, percent slope, rise:run ratio or gradians (the unit is read from the raster's geoprocessing history when it is recorded there, as Esri's Slope and Surface Parameters record it, and set in the Slope units drop-down) -- or a DEM, with What the raster holds set to Elevation (DEM), in which case the slope is computed from the elevations at each point.

Slope values (default): the raster already holds slope, in the unit chosen below. Elevation (DEM): the raster holds elevations and the tool computes the slope itself with the method chosen below (see Computing from a DEM in the usage notes); Slope units then give the unit of the computed values.

A new point feature class (a copy of the input): the input points are copied to the output feature class and the field is added to the copy. A new field in the input feature class: the field is added to the input itself and no copy is made; the output feature class parameter is then disabled. Only the points the layer shows receive values; other rows stay NULL.

The new point feature class: a copy of the input points with all their attributes plus the new slope field. A name is suggested from the input. Required when the values go to a new feature class; ignored when they go into the input.

param.name: interpolate
param.displayname: Interpolate values at the point locations (bilinear, on the slope angles)

dialogReference.para: Unchecked (default): each point gets the value of the cell it falls in, exactly as stored. Checked: each point gets a bilinear interpolation of the four surrounding cell centers computed on the slope angles (each cell converted to degrees first, averaged, converted back to the raster's unit), so a percent-slope raster interpolates correctly. NoData and out-of-range neighbors are excluded and the weights renormalized.

The name of the new DOUBLE field holding the extracted slope (default "Slope"). Adjusted automatically if the name is invalid for the workspace or already taken; the dialog warns when the input already has a field of that name.

param.name: slope_units
param.displayname: Slope units (of the raster, or of the values computed from a DEM)

dialogReference.para: The unit of the raster's slope values: Degrees (-90 to 90), Percent slope (100 times rise/run; 45 degrees = 100%; also called grade), Rise:run ratio, or Gradians (gons; 100 gon = 90 degrees). Defaults automatically from the raster's geoprocessing history (DEGREE or PERCENT_RISE recorded by Esri's Slope / Surface Parameters), falling back to Degrees. A unit chosen against that history draws a warning here and in the run report; the tool still runs with your choice. The extracted values are written in this unit; with interpolation on, the calculation passes through the slope angles and converts back. When the raster is a DEM this is simply the unit of the computed slope values.

Only when the raster is a DEM. Horn (3 x 3) (default): the third-order finite difference of Esri's Slope and Aspect tools, over true ground distances; on a true-to-scale projection it gives exactly the numbers Esri's planar tool gives. Quadratic least squares: the Evans-Young quadratic surface fitted to a window of cells (choose the size below), the slope taken from its first derivatives at the center; a wider window smooths noisy, fine-resolution DEMs.

The square window the quadratic surface is fitted to, 3 to 15 cells on a side (odd numbers). Only used with the quadratic method; Horn's method is always 3 x 3. Larger windows average over more terrain, as Esri's Surface Parameters neighborhood distance does.

The DEM's elevation unit, Meters or Feet. Set automatically, and locked, when the DEM has a vertical coordinate system that says; choose it yourself otherwise. A wrong unit scales every slope value, so check it when the DEM's metadata is silent.
For ModelBuilder: the input point features with their new field, filled in when the values are written into the input feature class (empty when a new feature class is made).

scriptExample.title: Extract Slope Values to Points example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Extract the containing-cell slope into a copy of the points, then an angle-space interpolated slope into a new field of the input itself. interpolate: True or False. write_to: "A new point feature class (a copy of the input)" or "A new field in the input feature class". slope_units: "Degrees (-90 to 90)", "Percent slope (rise/run × 100)", "Rise:run ratio", "Gradians (gons)". The new field is DOUBLE, in the raster's unit; NULL (geodatabase) or -9999 (shapefile) = NoData or outside the raster.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# Value of the cell each point falls in, written to a copy of the points arcpy.jenness.ExtractSlopeValuesToPoints( in_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points", in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\slope_percent", surface_type="Slope values", write_to="A new point feature class (a copy of the input)", out_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points_Slope", interpolate=False, field_name="Slope", slope_units="Percent slope (rise/run × 100)")
# Angle-space bilinear interpolation, written into the input feature class arcpy.jenness.ExtractSlopeValuesToPoints( in_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points", in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\slope_percent", surface_type="Slope values", write_to="A new field in the input feature class", interpolate=True, field_name="Slope_Pct", slope_units="Percent slope (rise/run × 100)")
# Slope straight from a DEM: Horn's 3 x 3 method, the numbers Esri's Slope tool gives arcpy.jenness.ExtractSlopeValuesToPoints( in_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points", in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\dem", surface_type="Elevation (DEM)", write_to="A new field in the input feature class", interpolate=False, field_name="Slope", slope_units="Degrees (-90 to 90)", slope_method="Horn (3 x 3; the method of Esri's Slope and Aspect tools)", elev_units="Meters")
# Quadratic least squares over a 7 x 7 window (smoother on a fine lidar DEM) arcpy.jenness.ExtractSlopeValuesToPoints( in_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points", in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\dem", surface_type="Elevation (DEM)", write_to="A new point feature class (a copy of the input)", out_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points_Slope", interpolate=True, field_name="Slope", slope_units="Percent slope (rise/run × 100)", slope_method="Quadratic least squares (choose the window size)", window_size=7, elev_units="Meters")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Adds a field with the slope at each point from a slope raster, to a copy of the points or to the input feature class itself; interpolation computed on the slope angles so percent slopes are never averaged raw; units detected from the raster's history; no Spatial Analyst.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Esri's Extract Values to Points for slope rasters. Percent slope is the tangent of the slope angle, a convex function, so averaging raw percent values biases an interpolated slope steep; with interpolation on, this tool converts the four surrounding cell centers to angles, interpolates bilinearly, and converts back to the raster's unit (degrees, percent, rise:run or gradians, read from the geoprocessing history when recorded there, with a warning when the chosen unit disagrees). The field goes to a copy of the input points or into the input feature class itself, under a name you choose. NoData and out-of-range neighbors are excluded with the weights renormalized; NoData or outside-the-raster points get NULL (geodatabase) or -9999 (shapefile). Points are read in the raster's coordinate system (the raster is never projected) and the raster is read only over the points' extent. One new DOUBLE field is added with full field-level metadata. No extension license is required.
